newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico to rebuy highways in rescue plan--analysts.
newsitem.headline: Mexico to rebuy highways in rescue plan--analysts.

text.p: The Mexican government is considering repurchasing freeway concessions it granted to different construction firms to help them cope with huge financial losses, analysts said on Thursday.
"It is my understanding that the government is trying to buy back the freeways," Goldman Sachs analyst Chris Hussey said. "The question is what percentage (of the projects) it buys."

Empresas ICA, Grupo Tribasa and Grupo Mexicano de Desarollo are among the firms that won concessions to build more than 3,750 miles (6,000 kilometers) of freeway during the 1988-1994 administration of former President Carlos Salinas.
The projects turned into a nightmare for the firms who paid fortunes for the concessions.
The companies' debt problems forced the Mexican government to budget this year about $3.3 billion to revive the freeways and give the constructors a badly-needed breather.

Analysts say the government's rescue program will soon be unveiled. They see the repurchase being made with a discount to the net economic value of each project, so that the building firms recover less than what they invested.
"The key question is what kind of discount the government will buy the concessions back at," Smith Barney analyst Carmen Slade wrote in a recent report.
Some analysts estimate that the discount will be applied equally to all companies and be in the range of 45 to 55 percent.
Mexican authorities and the construction companies have declined to comment on the contents of the program, but have said they will be announced soon.
The program could be revealed after the July 6 elections, analysts said, especially since the government's first restructuring plan put in place in June 1995 ended last month.
The analysts predicted the program would benefit ICA and Tribasa more than the GMD, because its investment in the toll roads represents a greater portion of the company's assets.
A strong discount to the concession value in the government's rescue plan could leave GMD almost bankrupt, ING Baring's Hector Castillo said.
